newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Buoyant Yeltsin reclaims power after surgery.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant Yeltsin reclaims power after surgery.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, surprising doctors with the pace of his recovery after quintuple heart bypass surgery, resumed full presidential duties on Wednesday, just 23 hours after the operation.

But U.S. cardiologist Michael DeBakey, who said after the operation that the 65-year-old Russian leader could be back on the tennis court in four months, urged him to be patient and follow his doctors' advice.
DeBakey advised the Russian team on Tuesday's operation.
Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had signed a decree taking back control over Russia at 6 a.m. (0300 GMT).
Power had been delegated to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin during the seven-hour operation and for the first hours after it.

"The patient's condition is stable, satisfactory, it corresponds to the gravity of the operation," Yastrzhembsky told a news conference, quoting a statement from the first meeting of Russian and foreign doctors after the surgery.
"All of us in the Kremlin are in a good mood because Boris Nikolayevich is recovering quickly, surprising the doctors with his strong health and powerful will," he added.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was pressing doctors hard to transfer him to the elite Central Clinical Hospital, where he was treated for past illnesses, apparently because he would feel more at home there.
"The president is chivvying the doctors (about a move) and he's keeping them on the defensive."
Yastrzhembsky said another doctors' meeting on Thursday would discuss Yeltsin's prospects of leaving the Cardiology Research Centre, where the operation was held.
DeBakey, speaking after visiting Yeltsin on Wednesday morning, said he was delighted by the president's condition.
"Everything is going quite well and of course it is very gratifying to see this happen because this is a very good sign that his prognosis is excellent," he told CNN television.
DeBakey, who pioneered bypass surgery in 1964, said he had warned Yeltsin not to take things too fast.
"I said 'You must be very patient, because I know that you want to get going'. But I said 'You know its very important that you follow the doctors' instructions'," DeBakey
He said Yeltsin could resume light duties in six to eight weeks and play tennis, one of his favourite hobbies before he fell ill four months ago, in three to four months.
"Within three or four months he could do almost anything he wants," DeBakey said.
The Kremlin said Chernomyrdin visited Yeltsin for 15 minutes to pass on good wishes and report on the state of the nation. Yeltsin said he was determined to return to work soon.

Yeltsin has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since he won a second term in office on July 3 and his prolonged illness has paralysed Russia's post-communist development, damaging Western investor confidence and unleashing a new bout of political infighting in the Kremlin.
The president's friends and foes were waiting to see whether he would take full control of the Kremlin or become a lame duck for his second term, due to end midway through the year 2000.
But for Wednesday the mood was one of conciliation. Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, Yeltsin's rival in the July presidential runoff, wished the president a speedy recovery.
"He must now care more about health," he told reporters. "He must trust more of the people he is working with, otherwise there will be neither health nor government."
Russian markets firmed on Wednesday on news of the operation and Russian debt prices opened stronger in London.
The Kremlin power vacuum has hampered government efforts to resolve a cash-flow crisis which means millions of public and private-sector workers have not been paid for months.
